div.head: II Atr 6.2
div.ab: ⁊ þæt naðor ne hy ne we ne underfon oðres wealh ne oðres ðeof ne oðres gefan.
Et ut nec ipsi neque nos alterius seruum uel inimicum receptemus.
⁊ þæt naðor ne hy ne we ne underfon oðres wealh ne oðres ðeof ne oðres gefan.
Und dass weder sie noch wir einen vom anderen [Contrahenten entlaufenen] Unfreien aufnehmen, noch den vom anderen [verfolgten] Dieb oder einen vom anderen in Rache Befehdeten.
And that neither they nor we receive the other's slave [run away from the other contracting party], nor the other's [pursued] thief, nor the other's enemy [at feud with him].
And neither of the two parties to the truce—neither they nor we—shall harbour a slave belonging to the other party, or a thief pursued by them, or anyone who is involved in vendetta with them.
And neither they nor we are to receive the other party’s slave, or thief, or person concerned in a feud.

note.seg: Der Strafe und der Unfreiheit (s. d. 5f.) entging man vór diesem Vertrage durch Überlaufen zum Feinde. Eine ähnliche Abmachung traf England kurz vór II Atr mit der Normandie; s. Gl Begünstigung 18. Schon AGu 5 beschränkte das Auswandern auch Höriger zwischen Dänen und Engländern

Before this treaty one escaped punishment and unfreedom (see that word 5f.) by going over to the enemy. England made a similar agreement with Normandy shortly before II Atr; see Gl Begünstigung 18. AGu 5 had already restricted the migration, even of bondmen, between Danes and English
Ende 10. Jhs. hat wealh die Bed. ‘Knecht’ schon ohne Nebensinn der ‘Walliser’ Herkunft; s. Toller s. v. II
At the end of the 10th cent. wealh already has the meaning ‘slave’ without the secondary sense of ‘Welsh’ origin; see Toller s. v. II
þeof lässt Q aus: dachte er an þeow, das mit wealh in anderem Sinne identisch sein kann?
Q omits þeof: was he thinking of þeow, which can be identical with wealh in another sense?
Erweitere die Übs.: ‘einen dem anderen [strafrechtlich oder in Rache] Feindlichen’; vgl. Gl friedlos 1n. 16
Expand the translation: ‘one hostile to the other [in criminal law or in vengeance]’; cf. Gl friedlos 1n. 16

Cf. A. and G. 5 and the close of a letter of Pope John XV who shortly before brought about a reconciliation between Æthelred and Duke Richard of Normandy: et de hominibus regis vel de inimicis suis nullum Richardus recipiat, nec rex de suis sine sigillo eorum (see Mem. of St Dunstan, ed. Stubbs, p. 398; Wm of Malmesbury, Gesta Reg., Rolls Series, i. pp. 192–3).
By the end of the tenth century wealh is frequently used for ‘slave’ without any reference to Celtic origin.
